name: flow-card
description:
One step of a flow that happens away from the main product. THREE screens across TWO services are this shape, which is what made it a unit rather than a component: avenID's device authorisation, my.aven.ceo's name check, and my.aven.ceo's passkey sign-in. Each one is a mark or a status glyph, an eyebrow, a heading, a description, sometimes a code to read aloud, an action, and a line saying who you are talking to.

It is a unit because these are the screens where a user is asked to TRUST something, and every element on them is doing that job. On avenID the status glyph was three hand-drawn inline SVGs in an `{#if}` chain — three chances to drift and no way for another surface to reuse them. On checkout the same screen leads with the brand mark instead, which is why `crest` is a slot: what goes at the top of a trust screen is a decision the surface makes, not one this unit should force.

base.$description: Centred and narrow. This screen has exactly one job and nothing else on it, so the measure is tight and the whole card is the focal point — the composition rule that an empty-ish screen owns its viewport rather than floating under a header.

eyebrow.$description: Composes `text--eyebrow`. Only the colour is this unit's; the size, weight, case and tracking come from the one definition.

code.$description: A code the user reads aloud or types into another device. Tabular, wide-tracked and grouped, because the failure mode here is misreading an 8 as a B — and `user-select: all` so one click selects the whole thing rather than half of it.

actions.$description: The affirmative action goes LAST — rightmost in a left-to-right reading order — and the way out goes first. That is the direction of travel: you read to the end of the row and the end is the thing you came to do. Putting the primary first means the eye lands on it before it has read what it is agreeing to, and it puts Cancel where the thumb expects Confirm.

trust.$description: Who you are actually talking to. On a screen whose whole purpose is being trusted, this is content and not a footer — it is the sentence that answers 'should I press this'.

crest.$description: What sits at the top of a trust screen — a status glyph on avenID, the brand mark on checkout. A slot rather than a fixed glyph, because those two surfaces are answering different questions: 'how is this going' and 'who is this'. The tinted disc is the same tint/ink pairing a badge uses, so a status here and a status in a table read as one system.

status.$description: The answer, in one word, at the size the eye lands on first — `taken`, `free`, `expired`. On checkout this was a bare `.status` with `.taken` and `.free` beside it, which is colour carrying the meaning; the WORD carries it here and the colour agrees with it.
Where the flow is. It dresses the CREST and nothing else — a whole card turning green says the page succeeded, when what succeeded is one step.

crest.$description: What the crest holds. `brand` drops the tinted disc entirely, because a logo inside a coloured circle is a logo with a badge around it.

answer.$description: The colour agreeing with the word, never replacing it.

step.$description: WHERE in the flow this card is — which is not the same as `status`, which is how it is GOING. Each step tints the eyebrow and the crest with the tone that belongs to it, so the four screens of one sequence are visibly one sequence rather than four cards that happen to look alike. Three of these once declared nothing at all and were documentation wearing a variant's name: a switch that changes nothing is worse than no switch, because it teaches you the control is broken.

identify.$description: Who are you — the name check, the sign-in.

authorise.$description: Do you allow this — the device grant, the consent.

pay.$description: Confirm the money. Marine, because this is the one step that takes something.

a11y.note: `aria-live="polite"` on the card, because the heading and description CHANGE as the flow advances and a screen-reader user is otherwise left on the previous step with no way to know. The alert is `role="alert"`, which interrupts — correct for a failure the user must act on. The status glyph is decorative: colour is never the only signal, so the heading always says in words what the glyph says in shape. The code is `user-select: all` so it can be copied in one gesture rather than dragged. The visual order and the DOM order are the same, so a keyboard tabs to the way out before the commit — which is the safer default when someone is moving fast.
